title: Linear programmes
objectives: Write a trading or allocation problem as a linear programme.

screens.title: The desk problem
screens.prose: A fund puts $x$ and $y$ (£m) into strategies A and B. It expects £60k and £40k of profit a year per £m. It has at most £10m. A uses 3 risk units per £m and B one, with 18 available. At most £5m fits in A. Drag P around the shaded plans.

derive.caption: P = ({{fixed(P.x, 1)}}, {{fixed(P.y, 1)}}): profit £{{fixed(60*P.x + 40*P.y, 0)}}k, {{(P.x + P.y > 10.0001 ? 'outside: over budget' : (3*P.x + P.y > 18.0001 ? 'outside: over the risk budget' : (P.x > 5.0001 ? 'outside: over the liquidity limit' : (P.x < -0.0001 || P.y < -0.0001 ? 'outside: negative' : 'inside'))))}}.

screens.question: Drag P to $(2, 5)$. What profit does that plan earn, in £k a year?

feedback.correct: £320k. Drag P across a line and the caption names the limit it breaks.

byKey.swap: You swapped the rates: $40 \times 2 + 60 \times 5 = 380$. A earns 60 per £m.
byKey.sum: You added the £m. Profit weights each by its rate.

explain.text: $60 \times 2 + 40 \times 5 = 320$, so the plan earns £320k a year. It sits inside every limit; plans outside the shading break at least one.

screens.title: Each limit is a line
screens.prose: Each sentence of the story is one straight line on the picture, with the allowed plans on one side.
screens.question: Match each limit to its line.

tokens.text: 3 risk units per £m of A, one per £m of B, 18 available

hints.text: The budget adds the two amounts.
Liquidity mentions A only, so it is a vertical line.

feedback.correct: The amounts $x$ and $y$ are the **decision variables** and $60x + 40y$ is a **linear objective**. The limits are **linear constraints**. The plans meeting all of them form the **feasible region**.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Read each sentence for which amounts it involves and with what weights.

byKey.t1: The total of $x$ and $y$ is the budget line $x + y = 10$.
byKey.t3: Only A is limited by liquidity: $x = 5$.

explain.text: The limits are $x + y \le 10$, $3x + y \le 18$ and $x \le 5$. With $x, y \ge 0$ they cut out the pentagon, the **feasible region**.

screens.title: From words to a constraint
screens.prose: A new limit: each £m of A uses 2 units of margin and each £m of B uses 4. The desk has 36 units.
screens.question: Write the margin used by a plan $(x, y)$.

hints.text: Margin used is $2x + 4y$, and the limit is $2x + 4y \le 36$.

feedback.correct: $2x + 4y \le 36$. It cuts off the corner $(0, 10)$, which uses 40 units. The best plan $(4, 6)$ uses only $8 + 24 = 32$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply each amount by its units per £m and add.

byKey.swap: You attached the 4 to $x$. A uses 2 units per £m and B uses 4.

explain.text: Units per £m times £m, added over the strategies: $2x + 4y$. The limit is $2x + 4y \le 36$, the dashed line.

screens.title: The general form
screens.prose: Every such problem reads $\max \mathbf{c}^T\mathbf{x}$ subject to $\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x} \le \mathbf{b}$, $\mathbf{x} \ge \mathbf{0}$. Here $\mathbf{c} = (60, 40)$, $\mathbf{b} = (10, 18, 5)$, and each row of $\mathbf{A}$ is one limit.
screens.question: What is the first column of $\mathbf{A}$, the coefficients of $x$ in the three limits?

hints.text: List the coefficient of $x$ in budget, risk and liquidity, in that order.
The column is $(1, 3, 1)$; the $y$ column is $(1, 1, 0)$.

feedback.correct: $(1, 3, 1)$. So $\mathbf{A} = \begin{pmatrix}1 & 1\\ 3 & 1\\ 1 & 0\end{pmatrix}$, one row per limit, one column per variable.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Read down the $x$ coefficients of the three limits.

byKey.row: That is the first row, the budget. A column runs down the limits.
byKey.ycol: That is the $y$ column: liquidity has no $y$.
byKey.length: Give one number per limit: three entries.

explain.text: $\mathbf{A} = \begin{pmatrix}1 & 1\\ 3 & 1\\ 1 & 0\end{pmatrix}$, so $\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x} \le \mathbf{b}$ stacks the three limits. Its first column holds what one £m of A uses of each limit.

screens.title: Slack
screens.prose: A **slack** variable measures room left: $s_1 = 10 - x - y$, $s_2 = 18 - 3x - y$, $s_3 = 5 - x$, each $\ge 0$. Each inequality becomes an equality with $s \ge 0$.
screens.question: Give the slacks $(s_1, s_2, s_3)$ at the plan $(4, 6)$.

hints.text: Subtract what the plan uses from each limit.
$(0, 0, 1)$: budget and risk are used up.

feedback.correct: $(0, 0, 1)$. Budget and risk are **active** at $(4, 6)$; £1m of liquidity room is unused.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compute $b_i$ minus what the plan uses of limit $i$.

byKey.used: Those are the amounts used, not the room left.
byKey.length: Give three slacks, one per limit.

explain.text: $s_1 = 10 - 4 - 6 = 0$, $s_2 = 18 - 12 - 6 = 0$ and $s_3 = 5 - 4 = 1$. A zero slack marks a limit the plan presses against.

screens.title: An execution problem
screens.prose: A trader must buy exactly 10,000 shares across three venues. Let $a$, $b$, $c$ be the shares sent to each.
screens.question: Which linear programme describes the cheapest split?

options.text: $\min 0.30a + 0.25b + 0.40c$ s.t. $a + b + c \le 10{,}000$ and the capacities
options.why: With $\le$ the cheapest plan buys nothing. The order must be filled: an equality.

options.text: $\max 0.30a + 0.25b + 0.40c$ s.t. $a + b + c = 10{,}000$ and the capacities
options.why: That finds the most expensive split. Fees are to be minimised.

hints.text: What must the three amounts add to?
Exactly 10,000: an equality, not a limit.
Minimise fees, with an equality for the total and bounds for the capacities.

feedback.correct: An equality for the total and a bound per venue. The problem has three variables and is still linear.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. The order must be filled exactly, at the lowest fees.

byKey.le: That allows $a = b = c = 0$, which costs nothing and fills nothing.
byKey.max: Maximising fees is the wrong direction.

explain.text: The total is an equality row and each capacity is a bound $0 \le a_i \le u_i$. The objective is the fee bill in pence, to be minimised.

screens.title: At least, not at most
screens.prose: A hedge buys $a$ and $b$ futures costing £1.0k and £1.5k each. They cover $(2, 1)$ and $(1, 3)$ of two risk factors per contract, and the book needs at least $(8, 9)$. Minimise $1.0a + 1.5b$ (£k).
screens.question: What does the cheapest hedge cost, in pounds?

canvas.caption: With $\le$ rows the region is this small corner, and $(0, 0)$ costs nothing.

hints.text: The region is unbounded upwards; its corners are $(0, 8)$, $(3, 2)$ and $(9, 0)$.

feedback.correct: £6,000 at $(3, 2)$. "At least" rows point away from the origin, so doing nothing is not allowed.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Price the three corners of the region where both cover rows hold.

byKey.flip: You wrote the rows with $\le$, so buying nothing "wins" at £0. The book needs at least $(8, 9)$ of cover.
byKey.corner: £9,000 is the corner $(9, 0)$. The corner $(3, 2)$ is cheaper.
byKey.corner2: £12,000 is the corner $(0, 8)$. Mixing both contracts is cheaper.

explain.text: Solving $2a + b = 8$ and $a + 3b = 9$ gives $(3, 2)$, costing $3 + 3 = 6$, so £6,000. With the rows reversed the region flips to the corner at the origin, and the "best" hedge buys nothing.

screens.title: No best plan
screens.prose: Drop the budget and the risk limit and keep only $x \le 5$ with $x, y \ge 0$. Maximise $60x + 40y$.

state.caption: The strip runs up for ever.

screens.question: What is the best profit?

options.text: There is none: profit grows without limit as $y$ grows.

options.why: You assumed $y = 0$. Nothing stops $y$ from growing.
That needed the budget and the risk limit, which are gone.

feedback.correct: Unbounded: no plan is best. Add $x + y \ge 12$ to the full desk instead and no plan is feasible at all.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check whether any limit stops $y$.

byKey.x5: $(5, 100)$ earns £4,300k. There is always a better plan.
byKey.old: Without the budget and risk limits $(4, 6)$ is not special.

explain.text: With only $x \le 5$ the profit $60x + 40y$ grows without bound in $y$: the LP is **unbounded**. With $x + y \ge 12$ and $x + y \le 10$ together it is **infeasible**.

screens.title: The cheapest split
screens.prose: Back to the 10,000 shares. The cheapest fee is at venue 2, then venue 1, then venue 3.
screens.question: Fill the cheapest venues first. What is the total fee bill, in pounds?

hints.text: Venue 2 takes 3,000 at 0.25p; venue 1 takes 4,000 at 0.30p.

feedback.correct: 3,150p, £31.50, with the split $(4{,}000, 3{,}000, 3{,}000)$. Lesson 6 shows why this is a corner, and lesson 7 solves it in code.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Fill venue 2, then venue 1, then put the rest at venue 3.

byKey.pence: 3,150 is the bill in pence. In pounds it is £31.50.
byKey.cheap: £25 would need all 10,000 at 0.25p, but venue 2 takes only 3,000.
byKey.all3: £40 sends all 10,000 to the dearest venue.

ideas: A linear programme has decision variables, a linear objective and linear constraints. The plans meeting every constraint form the feasible region.

In matrix form it is $\max \mathbf{c}^T\mathbf{x}$ subject to $\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x} \le \mathbf{b}$, $\mathbf{x} \ge \mathbf{0}$, with one row of $\mathbf{A}$ per limit. Slacks are $\mathbf{b} - \mathbf{A}\mathbf{x} \ge \mathbf{0}$.
An "at least" row becomes $\le$ after multiplying by $-1$. A programme can be unbounded or infeasible.
summary.trap: Writing an "at least" cover row with $\le$ makes buying nothing look optimal.

quiz.prose: A colleague writes the risk limit as $x + 3y \le 18$, attaching the 3 to the wrong strategy. The best plan becomes $(5, \tfrac{13}{3})$.
quiz.question: What profit does that plan report, in £k?

byKey.right: £480k is the right model's answer. The swapped row moves the optimum to $(5, \tfrac{13}{3})$.

explain.text: With $x + 3y \le 18$ the corner is $x = 5$, $y = \tfrac{13}{3}$, earning £473.33k. The plan also breaks the real risk limit: $3 \times 5 + \tfrac{13}{3} > 18$.

quiz.prose: The desk adds a rule: invest at least £12m, $x + y \ge 12$, while keeping the budget $x + y \le 10$.
quiz.question: What happens to the linear programme?

options.text: It is infeasible: no plan meets both rules.

options.why: Unbounded means plans with ever larger profit. Here there is no plan at all.
$(4, 6)$ invests £10m, below the new floor of £12m.

feedback.correct: Infeasible: $x + y$ cannot be both at least 12 and at most 10.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Can any plan satisfy both rows?

explain.text: The two rows contradict each other, so the feasible region is empty. A solver reports infeasible rather than a plan.

quiz.prose: Take the plan $(5, 3)$ on the desk problem.
quiz.question: What are its slacks $(s_1, s_2, s_3)$ for budget, risk and liquidity?

feedback.correct: $(2, 0, 0)$: risk and liquidity are active, £2m of budget is unused.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Subtract what the plan uses from each limit.

quiz.prose: A pension scheme must hold at least £2m of gilts, $g$. It must also hold at least twice as much in gilts as in equities, $e$.
quiz.question: Which pair of rows says this in the form $\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x} \le \mathbf{b}$?

options.why: You kept the directions of "at most". Multiply an "at least" row by $-1$ to turn it round.
That says $e \le 2g$: you put the 2 on the wrong asset. The rule is $g \ge 2e$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Write each rule with $\ge$ first, then multiply by $-1$.

explain.text: An "at least" row $\mathbf{a}^T\mathbf{x} \ge \beta$ is $-\mathbf{a}^T\mathbf{x} \le -\beta$. Getting the direction wrong flips the region, as the hedge showed.
